hook.line: Some things hurt, and it has nothing to do with your body. Don Hernando knows this one well whenever the talk turns to Rosa.
hook.es: Me duele que Rosa no esté aquí.
hook.en: It hurts that Rosa isn't here.

examples.es: Me duele que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.
examples.en: It hurts that Altamira says that about Rosa.
It hurts not to be able to help you. (to a friend)

examples.es: Me duele mucho que Rosa no esté.
examples.en: It hurts me a lot that Rosa isn't here.

examples.es: ¿Te duele que Tomás no hable con ellos?
examples.en: Does it hurt you that Tomás doesn't talk to them? (to a friend)

examples.es: A Vale le duele que don Hernando no venga.
examples.en: It hurts Vale that don Hernando isn't coming.

rule:
It's the same backwards grammar as *me duele la cabeza*: what hurts is the subject, and *me, te, le, nos* say who feels it.

Someone else's action: *que* plus the wish form. *Me duele que no me hable.*
Your own inability: the infinitive. *Me duele no poder ayudarte.*

With *que* it's always *duele*, never *duelen*. It's heavier than *me da pena*: it's about hurt feelings, not just sadness.
smallPrint: Teachers still call *doler* a *gustar*-type verb, even when the pain is emotional.

options: It hurts that you can't help me.
It hurts me not to be able to help you.
It hurts that she can't help you.

options: It hurts that you can't help me. (to a friend)
It hurts me not to be able to help you.

options: Does it hurt Tomás that you don't talk to them?
Does Tomás hurt you?
Does it hurt you that Tomás doesn't talk to them? (to a friend)

options: It hurts me that Rosa isn't here.
It hurts us that Rosa isn't here.
It hurts Rosa that we aren't here.

It hurts that you don't see me.
It hurts that I don't see her.

readAndPick.es: Me duele que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.

It hurts that Altamira says that about Rosa.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *dice* or *diga* and type the whole sentence: *Me duele que Altamira ___ eso de Rosa.*
yourTurn.answer: Me duele que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.
yourTurn.why: A feeling about someone else's action takes the wish form: *diga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It hurts not to be able to help you. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: It's your own inability, so no *que*: just *no poder*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It hurts me a lot that Rosa isn't here.
yourTurn.answer: Me duele mucho que Rosa no esté aquí.
accept: Me duele mucho que Rosa no esté.
yourTurn.why: *Mucho* goes right after *duele*, and *esté* is the wish form of *estar*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Vale: *Me duele que don Hernando no venga.*
yourTurn.answer: A Vale le duele que don Hernando no venga.
yourTurn.why: *Me* becomes *le*, and *A Vale* says who feels it.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: Does it hurt you that Tomás doesn't talk to them?
yourTurn.answer: ¿Te duele que Tomás no hable con ellos?
yourTurn.why: *Te* is you, and *hable* is the wish form of *hablar*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about all of us: *Me duele que Rosa no esté.*
yourTurn.answer: Nos duele que Rosa no esté.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It hurts me not to see you. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: Your own action, so the infinitive, and *te* attaches to the end: *verte*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me duele que no puedo ayudarte.
pitfalls.why: Almost. When it's your own inability, there's no *que*: use the infinitive.

pitfalls.wrong: Yo duelo que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.
pitfalls.right: Me duele que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.
pitfalls.why: The event is what hurts, so you become *me* and the verb is *duele*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me duele que Altamira dice eso de Rosa.
pitfalls.right: Me duele que Altamira diga eso de Rosa.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *me duele que*, the verb takes the wish form: *diga*.

personal: Tell us about something someone does, or doesn't do, that hurts. For example: *Me duele que mis amigos no me llamen.* or *Me duele no ver a mi familia.*
